claims.text: Disk-averaged total-gas measurements across normal spirals and starbursts yield a super-linear global Schmidt-Kennicutt relation with an index near 1.4.
On sub-kiloparsec scales in nearby disks, star-formation-rate surface density correlates closely with CO-traced molecular gas and is largely uncorrelated with atomic hydrogen.
In molecule-dominated nearby disks the molecular star-formation relation is near-linear with a narrow molecular depletion time of order 1-2 Gyr.
Atomic hydrogen surface density saturates near 9-10 solar masses per square parsec, with much lower star-formation efficiency in HI-dominated outer disks.
Integrated infrared luminosity correlates approximately linearly with dense-gas (HCN) luminosity across galaxies and extends to massive Milky Way clumps.
Nearby molecular clouds form stars inefficiently relative to their free-fall time, with recent star formation concentrated in high-extinction dense gas.
The CO-to-H2 conversion factor is environment-dependent, varying with metallicity, radiation field, temperature, and dynamics.
Whether high-redshift disks and extreme starbursts occupy two offset star-formation sequences or a single continuous law is unresolved.
claims.debate_topic: Discrete disk/starburst sequences vs a continuous star-formation law

claims.text: The form of CO-to-H2 variation is contested between a two-value (Galactic/starburst) prescription and continuous environmental variation.
claims.debate_topic: Magnitude and form of alpha_CO variation

claims.text: Whether molecular hydrogen is causally required for collapse or merely co-locates with shielded cold gas remains unresolved.
claims.debate_topic: Causal role of H2 in star formation

sections.section: The Star-Forming Main Sequence and Quenching

claims.text: Most star-forming galaxies occupy a relatively narrow SFR-stellar-mass main sequence with scatter of order 0.3 dex out to at least z~2.5.
The galaxy population is bimodal, separating into a star-forming blue cloud and a quiescent red sequence.
Reproducing the massive quenched galaxy population requires preventive suppression of cooling and star formation in massive halos beyond low-mass stellar feedback.
Stellar feedback-driven outflows are required to lower the efficiency of low-mass galaxies and transport metals out of star-forming disks.
The global molecular depletion time is not a single constant but correlates with specific SFR and offset from the main sequence.
Whether massive-galaxy quenching is set by virial heating and black-hole feedback or by overlapping environmental and gas-supply processes is unresolved.
Whether quenching proceeds by reduced supply/exhaustion, suppressed star-formation efficiency at fixed gas, or rapid gas removal is debated.
claims.debate_topic: Quenching pathway: supply vs efficiency vs removal

claims.text: Molecular-gas fractions rise steeply from the local Universe to cosmic noon while the molecular depletion time evolves more weakly.
At low redshift, atomic and molecular gas fractions vary systematically with stellar mass, color/specific SFR, and surface density, with different dependences for the two phases.
The observed growth of stellar mass cannot be supplied by the declining HI+H2 reservoirs alone, requiring continued net accretion of gas.
Gas accretion separates into rapidly cooling cold/filamentary and shock-heated hot-halo pathways, with the balance set by halo mass, redshift, and environment.
Whether cold filamentary accretion or hot-mode shocked cooling dominates galaxy growth is unresolved.
Whether outflowing gas is permanently ejected or substantially recycled through galactic fountains and the CGM is unresolved.
The cosmic star-formation-rate density rises from the present to a broad maximum near z~2 and declines toward higher redshift.
Roughly half of today's stellar mass had formed by z~1.3 and about a quarter above z~2.
Dust-obscured, infrared-emitting star formation is a major and near cosmic-noon dominant component of the total star-formation budget.
The cosmic molecular-gas density rises toward cosmic noon and declines afterward, mirroring the cosmic star-formation-rate density.
The observed stellar-mass-density history is broadly consistent with the time integral of the SFR density after stellar mass return, with a residual offset.
Salpeter- and Chabrier-like initial mass functions imply materially different SFR normalizations, mass-return fractions, and metal yields.
Whether the decline of the SFR density at z>6 is largely physical or amplified by galaxies below detection limits is unresolved.
Whether a universal IMF is justified for cross-epoch comparison, versus environment- or metallicity-dependent forms, is debated.
The local gas-phase mass-metallicity relation rises with stellar mass and flattens above a turnover near 10^10.5 solar masses, with scatter of order 0.1 dex.
Mean stellar metallicity rises with stellar mass as a distinct integrated-history relation separate from the gas-phase abundance.
The gas-phase mass-metallicity relation normalization declines toward higher redshift out to at least z~3.3.
Strong-line metallicity calibration families disagree by up to about 0.7 dex in absolute oxygen abundance even where relative trends agree.
Effective yields in low-mass galaxies fall below closed-box expectations, consistent with inflow and/or preferential metal loss.
Most local non-interacting star-forming disks show negative radial gas-phase abundance gradients.
The reality, strength, and redshift-invariance of a fundamental metallicity relation linking mass, SFR, and metallicity are disputed.
claims.debate_topic: Reality and universality of the FMR

claims.text: What physically sets the mass-metallicity relation, among mass-dependent outflow, inflow dilution, star-formation efficiency, and retention, is model-dependent and unresolved.
Whether the low-mass mass-metallicity relation slope evolves into the JWST high-redshift regime is debated.
The closed-box model is a useful null hypothesis but fails the G-dwarf problem, requiring gas infall and finite stellar delays.
Core-collapse supernovae deliver prompt alpha-element enrichment while Type Ia supernovae add iron-peak elements over a broad delay-time distribution.
The [alpha/Fe] ratio encodes the duration and timing of star formation, with high values indicating rapid early formation before delayed iron enrichment.
Low- and intermediate-mass stars return carbon, nitrogen, and s-process elements through the AGB phase on mass-dependent delays.
The N/O ratio shows a low-metallicity plateau that rises at higher O/H, consistent with primary nitrogen plus delayed secondary production.
Gas-regulator models express galaxy metallicity as a balance among inflow, star formation, recycling, yields, and outflow rather than a closed-box clock.
The progenitor channels of Type Ia supernovae are debated even though the near-t^-1 delay-time-distribution shape is comparatively secure.
claims.debate_topic: Type Ia progenitors and delay-time distribution

claims.text: Whether [alpha/Fe] is driven purely by star-formation timing or also by IMF variation and metallicity-dependent yields is unresolved.
The evolution of radial abundance gradients at z~1-3 is contested because beam smearing and inflow can mimic flat or inverted profiles.
The circumgalactic medium is gas outside a galaxy's stellar disk and ISM but within its virial radius, multiphase in ionization and complex in kinematics.
Cool, HI-bearing circumgalactic gas is common around both star-forming and passive low-redshift galaxies.
Photoionization modeling implies a large cool-CGM baryonic reservoir of order 10^10-10^11 solar masses around L-star galaxies.
Strong O VI absorption is widespread around star-forming L-star galaxies and much weaker around passive galaxies.
A substantial fraction of the metals produced by a galaxy resides outside its stellar disk.
The circumgalactic medium acts as a reservoir and transfer medium for accretion, feedback, and recycling that regulates the galaxy gas supply.
Whether small cool CGM clouds are rapidly shredded by the hot halo or survive and regenerate through cooling, conduction suppression, or magnetic fields is unresolved.
Whether O VI arises in collisionally ionized ~10^5.5 K gas or in photoionized and non-equilibrium interfaces is debated.
claims.debate_topic: O VI ionization mechanism and temperature

claims.text: Whether the detected cool and warm phases close the CGM baryon budget or large hot and low-density reservoirs remain unmeasured is unresolved.

sections.section: The Cosmic Baryon and Metal Census

claims.text: More than 90 percent of cosmic baryons remain gaseous rather than locked in stars at the present epoch.
Big-Bang-nucleosynthesis and CMB-anisotropy estimates give concordant total baryon-density normalizations.
The comoving neutral-atomic-gas density evolves only modestly from z~5 to the present.
At z>2.5 the metal mass in cold gas can account for nearly all metals expected from the integrated star-formation history, while at z<1 stars are the largest identified metal reservoir.
The dust-to-metals ratio is not universal and decreases toward low metallicity.
Whether the cosmic metal census is genuinely closed or a residual population hides in poorly measured warm-hot phases is unresolved.
How much ionization corrections in CGM and Lyman-limit gas bias inferred total masses under an uncertain radiation field is debated.

Both semi-analytic models and cosmological hydrodynamic simulations begin from hierarchical dark-matter assembly and add baryonic cooling, star formation, feedback, enrichment, and structural evolution.
The shallow abundance of low-mass galaxies relative to the halo mass function requires strongly mass-dependent suppression of baryon conversion in shallow potential wells.
Abundance matching places peak stellar-conversion efficiency near Milky-Way-scale (~10^12 solar-mass) halos, with lower efficiency on both sides.
Because cosmological volumes cannot resolve the multiphase ISM, both model families rely on subgrid star-formation and feedback prescriptions.
Depositing supernova thermal energy directly at insufficient resolution produces numerical overcooling unless mitigated.
Different wind implementations (kinetic kicks, thermal deposition, or effective equations of state) reproduce the required regulation through different paths.
Subgrid degeneracy means numerical convergence is not physical validation, as different recipes yield similar calibrations but divergent mechanisms.
The dominant stellar-feedback channel, supernovae versus radiation, photoionization, and pre-supernova winds, is contested.
Mergers, dissipative gas dynamics, and internal disk instabilities can all build bulges, compactness, and spheroids.
Halo angular momentum and the retention or loss of baryons provide a baseline connection between halo properties and disk sizes.
Star-forming and quiescent galaxy populations follow different mass-normalized size evolution out to z~3.
Early cooling-only simulations overproduced central stellar mass and lost too much baryonic angular momentum, motivating stronger regulation and improved numerical treatment.
Whether major and minor mergers or internal secular and violent-disk-instability processes dominate spheroid and compact-galaxy growth is unresolved.
Whether galaxy sizes chiefly reflect halo spin with approximate angular-momentum conservation or are set by feedback-selective loss, torques, and accretion history is debated.
